name: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
description: A large-scale dataset for object detection and segmentation in natural context. Contains photos of 91 object types that would be easily recognizable by a 4 year old, with 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization. The dataset focuses on detecting non-iconic views of objects, contextual reasoning between objects, and precise 2D localization.
creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
citeAs: T. Lin, M. Maire, S. Belongie, J. Hays, P. Perona, D. Ramanan, P. Dollár, and C. L. Zitnick,
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from Flickr using a novel pipeline. Rather than searching for object categories in isolation (which tends to return iconic images), the authors searched for pairwise combinations of object categories (e.g., 'dog + car') and scene/object category pairs to find natural images containing multiple objects in their natural context. At most 5 photos taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. In rare cases where enough images could not be found using pairs, single category searches were performed with explicit filtering to remove iconic images. The result is a collection of 328,000 images with rich contextual relationships between objects.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were sourced from Flickr, a photo-sharing platform containing photos uploaded by amateur photographers with searchable metadata and keywords. Images were retrieved using queries for pairwise combinations of object categories and scene/object category pairs.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: An explicit filtering stage was performed to remove iconic images when single category searches were used. Near-duplicate images were removed using detection algorithms, and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize the chance of near-duplicate images existing across train/validation/test splits.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation pipeline consisted of three primary stages using Amazon Mechanical Turk workers: (1) Category labeling: Workers indicated which object categories were present in each image using a hierarchical approach with 11 super-categories. For each category found, workers dragged the category's icon onto one instance of the category. 8 workers labeled each image. (2) Instance spotting: Workers placed a cross on top of each instance of a specific category (up to 10 instances per category per image). The location from the previous stage was shown to prime workers. 8 workers labeled each image. (3) Instance segmentation: Workers segmented each object instance using a modified version of the OpenSurfaces interface. All workers were required to complete a training task for each object category before being allowed to segment instances - workers could not complete the training until their segmentation adequately matched ground truth. This filtered out approximately 2 in 3 workers. Each instance was segmented by a single worker. A verification step was then performed where 3-5 workers judged each segmentation; segmentations receiving fewer than 4 of 5 favorable votes were discarded and re-segmented. For images with more than 10-15 instances of a category, remaining instances were marked as 'crowds' using a single segment rather than individual segmentations.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For category labeling, a category was considered present if any of the 8 workers indicated it; false positives were handled in subsequent stages. The authors analyzed worker quality by comparing 7 expert workers (co-authors) with unions of 1-10 AMT workers. The union of 8 AMT workers achieved greater recall than any individual expert. Worker recall saturated at around 9-10 AMT workers. For any unambiguous examples with over 50% probability of being annotated, the probability all 8 annotators would miss it was at most 0.004. The authors estimate over 99% of all object categories not later rejected as false positives were detected given 8 annotators. For segmentation verification, each segmentation was initially shown to 3 annotators; if any indicated it was bad, it was shown to 2 additional workers. Segmentations not receiving at least 4 of 5 favorable votes were discarded.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Category labeling: 8 workers per image. Instance spotting: 8 workers per image. Instance segmentation: 1 worker per instance, with 3-5 workers for verification.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The MS COCO dataset is split into two roughly equal parts. The first half was released in 2014, containing 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The second half was planned for release in 2015, bringing the cumulative total to 165,482 train, 81,208 val, and 81,434 test images. Annotations for train and validation data are released, but not for test. An evaluation server for automatic evaluation on the test set was being finalized at the time of publication. The 2014 release was limited to a subset of 80 categories (11 categories were excluded), with potential addition of segmentations for some excluded categories in the cumulative 2015 release.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset currently only labels 'things' (objects for which individual instances may be easily labeled) and not 'stuff' categories (materials and objects with no clear boundaries like sky, street, grass). The authors note that labeling 'stuff' categories could provide significant contextual information useful for detection. The dataset is limited to entry-level categories (commonly used category labels like 'dog', 'chair', 'person') rather than fine-grained categories (e.g., 'German shepherd') or object-part categories (e.g., 'face', 'hands', 'wheels'), though the authors note these could be beneficial for real-world applications. The 2014 release excluded 11 categories: hat, shoe, eyeglasses (too many instances), mirror, window, door, street sign (ambiguous and difficult to label), plate, desk (confusion with bowl and dining table), blender, and hair brush (too few instances).
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for object detection and segmentation tasks. It can be used for training, testing, and validation of object recognition algorithms. The dataset is particularly suited for: (1) detecting non-iconic views of objects in natural contexts, (2) contextual reasoning between objects, and (3) precise 2D localization of objects using instance-level segmentation masks. The authors provide baseline performance analysis using Deformable Parts Models for both bounding box detection and segmentation tasks.
